title: Five More NHL Winners Than the Market, and Still Worse: Grading a Forecast With the Brier Score
excerpt: A model that never sees the price named 176 NHL winners to the market's 171, then lost on Brier score. Why right-or-wrong misleads, in Python.
content:
The NHL season opened on September 29 with the Florida Panthers in Carolina. The CQ blind model, the one on CrystlQuant that never sees a market price, gave Carolina a 75.0% chance. The market's closing price gave Carolina 54.1%. Florida won 1-0.

So both forecasts were wrong. Graded the way most people grade a forecast, right or wrong, they were wrong by exactly the same amount: one miss each. That feels unfair the moment you say it out loud. One of them said "probably Carolina". The other said "Carolina, three times in four". Those aren't the same mistake.

I help build CrystlQuant, a free sports forecasting site that puts a number on every game before it starts and grades every one afterwards, misses included. Grading in public forces you to decide what "graded" means, and that turns out to be a programming question with a surprising answer. Here it is, with the code and this season's hockey numbers.

## Counting winners

The obvious grade is accuracy: did the side you made the favorite win?

```python
def accuracy(probs, outcomes):
    # probs: chance the home team wins; outcomes: 1 if it did, 0 if not
    hits = sum((p > 0.5) == (y == 1) for p, y in zip(probs, outcomes))
    return hits / len(probs)
```

From that opening night through the games of November 8, there were 282 NHL regular-season games with a closing market price. By this measure the blind model had a fine autumn. It named the winner in 176 of them. The market named 171. Five more winners than the price that thousands of people with real money set, from a model that never looks at it.

If accuracy were the whole story, that would be the headline. It isn't, and the code above shows why. The function throws the probability away on its first line. A 51% call and a 99% call that land on the same side count the same. A forecaster could print 100% on every favorite and score exactly what it scores at 55%. Accuracy grades the pick. It doesn't grade the number, and the number is the thing we publish.

## The Brier score

In 1950 a weather forecaster named Glenn Brier proposed a fix that is still the standard. For each game, take the probability you gave the side that won, subtract it from 1, and square it. Average over all games. Lower is better.

```python
def brier(probs, outcomes):
    return sum((p - y) ** 2 for p, y in zip(probs, outcomes)) / len(probs)

brier([0.750], [0])   # 0.5625  the blind model on opening night
brier([0.541], [0])   # 0.2927  the market
brier([0.5], [0])     # 0.25    "no idea", either way
```

Now opening night looks like what it was. The market's miss cost 0.29. The blind model's cost 0.56, almost twice as much. Saying 50% on everything scores 0.25 whatever happens, so that's the line any forecaster has to get under to be saying something at all.

Over the same 282 games, here's the grade:

| Forecast | Winners named | Brier score |
|---|---|---|
| The market | 171 | 0.2257 |
| CrystlQuant | 176 | 0.2260 |
| The CQ blind model | 176 | 0.2278 |

Five more winners, and a worse score. Both can be true at once, because they're measuring different things. A second scoring rule, log loss, agrees with Brier: 0.6426 for the market, 0.6474 for the blind model.

## Why the square, and why it's honest

The square isn't decoration. It makes the Brier score what statisticians call a proper scoring rule: you get your best expected score by printing exactly what you believe. Here's the check in code. Suppose you really think a team wins 60% of the time:

```python
def expected_brier(say, believe):
    return believe * (1 - say) ** 2 + (1 - believe) * say ** 2

expected_brier(0.6, believe=0.6)   # 0.24
expected_brier(1.0, believe=0.6)   # 0.40
expected_brier(0.5, believe=0.6)   # 0.25
```

Round up to a confident 100% and your expected score gets much worse. Hedge down to 50% and it gets slightly worse. The only number that wins is the true one. Accuracy has no such property, so a forecaster graded on accuracy alone has no reason to get the number right, only the side. That's a bad incentive to build a product on.

## Three traps we hit writing it

**The factor of two.** Brier's original definition sums the squared error over every possible outcome, not only the one that happened. For a game with two outcomes that's exactly double the version above. When I first ran this season's numbers, the blind model came out at 0.4557 and I spent a minute wondering how anything could be that bad. It wasn't. It was the other definition. Pick one, write it in the function's docstring, and never compare a score from one with a score from the other. For football, where the draw is a third outcome, you need the multi-outcome form anyway, so the choice is a real one.

**Log loss can be infinite.** Log loss charges you the negative log of the probability you gave what happened. Give 0% to something that happens and that's the log of zero. In plain Python, `math.log(0)` stops the program with an error. In NumPy it returns minus infinity with a warning that's easy to miss, and one careless 100% turns the whole season's average into inf.

```python
import math

def log_loss(probs, outcomes, eps=1e-15):
    total = 0.0
    for p, y in zip(probs, outcomes):
        p = min(max(p, eps), 1 - eps)   # clip, or one 100% miss breaks it
        total -= math.log(p if y == 1 else 1 - p)
    return total / len(probs)
```

Clipping is the standard fix, but write down that you did it, because it's a choice. Brier has no such cliff. Its worst single game costs 1, which is one reason it's easier to put in front of readers.

**The 50% that picks a side by accident.** Look at `p > 0.5` in the accuracy function. A forecast of exactly 50% counts as a pick for the away team, silently. It almost never comes up with real numbers, and CrystlQuant's pages always show a decimal near 50 so the side is visible, but a grader should decide what an exact 50 means rather than let a comparison operator decide it.

## Where the blind model actually lost

Here's the part I didn't expect. In 53 of the 282 games, the blind model and the market named different winners. The blind model won those arguments 29 to 24, and it won them on the Brier score too. When it disagreed with the market, it was right more often and it was right by enough.

All of the damage came from the other 229 games, the ones where both named the same winner. Right side, different number. The blind model sat on average 4.4 points away from the market's price, and in 18 games it was 10 points or more away. When it was further from 50 than the market and the favorite lost, the square did its work. Opening night alone, a game where both forecasts made Carolina the favorite, accounts for 45% of the blind model's whole gap to the market over the season so far.

That's the real lesson of grading a probability rather than a pick. A forecast isn't only a side. Every game where you agree with everyone else still says how sure you are, and every one of those is scored.

## What CrystlQuant's numbers say

They say nobody beats the market. One model never sees the market price. The other fixes it.

The blind model is the raw read. It wins its arguments with the market and gives the points back on confidence. CrystlQuant starts where the market is, sits on average 0.74 points from its price, and moves only where it has reason to. Through November 8 it named 176 winners too, five more than the market, and gave back almost none of the market's sharpness on the way: a Brier score of 0.2260 to the market's 0.2257.

That gap lives in the fourth decimal place, and it's still the market's lead, so I'll say it plainly: by the score that grades the number, not the pick, the market is ahead of us in hockey this season by a hair. CrystlQuant is the forecast I'd take, because it names more winners and pays almost nothing for them, and the hair is the target. Every game on the board is graded in the open, misses included, on [CrystlQuant's record](https://crystlquant.com/record), so you can watch whether it closes.
